extracted.intended_audience: scholars, sociologists, scientists, and policymakers interested in the institutional norms/ethos of science
extracted.subtask_description: Identify and apply the normative standards Merton describes as constituting the ethos of modern science (universalism, communism, disinterestedness, organized skepticism) and related technical/institutional imperatives for assessing scientific behavior and institutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institutional goal of science
rubrics_metrics.description: The institutional goal of science is the extension of certified knowledge; technical methods are employed toward empirically confirmed and logically consistent statements of regularities (predictions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The goal provides rationale for mores and technical norms: norms derive from the goal and methods; evaluation of scientific activity should measure contribution toward reliable, predictive, empirically confirmed, and logically consistent knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technical norm: empirical evidence (adequate and reliable)
rubrics_metrics.description: The technical norm of empirical evidence, adequate and reliable, is a prerequisite for sustained true prediction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims must be consonant with observation and previously confirmed knowledge; verifiability and testability are emphasized. Anti-patterns: claims lacking adequate empirical support; secrecy or suppression that prevents verification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technical norm: logical consistency
rubrics_metrics.description: The technical norm of logical consistency is a prerequisite for systematic and valid prediction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scientific formulations should be logically coherent and consistent with accepted knowledge. Evaluate whether reasoning and inferential structure conform to accepted logical standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Universalism
rubrics_metrics.description: Truth-claims, whatever their source, are to be subjected to preestablished impersonal criteria; acceptance or rejection must not depend on the personal or social attributes of the claimant (race, nationality, religion, class, personal qualities are irrelevant).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Also expressed as the demand that careers be open to talents: access to scientific pursuits must be determined by competence, not status. Anti-patterns and tensions: ethnocentrism, nationalistic bias, caste-standards, partisan attacks cloaked in scientific language; lip service to universalism alongside practical exclusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Communism (communalism) of scientific knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: The substantive findings of science are a product of social collaboration and are assigned to the community; scientific knowledge is common heritage and is not the exclusive private property of discoverers beyond recognition/esteem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect and evaluate open contribution to the commonwealth of science; eponymy (naming) functions as recognition, not proprietary control. Anti-patterns: attempts to privatize knowledge, treat findings as exclusive property, or suppress results for private advantage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imperative for communication / anti-secrecy
rubrics_metrics.description: Full and open communication of findings is an institutional imperative; secrecy is the antithesis of the scientific norm of communism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publication and dissemination are morally compelled; withholding important discoveries is condemned. Examples: Henry Cavendish's modesty seen as anti-social; tension noted with patenting and secrecy. Evaluate whether findings are shared promptly and openly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Priority and recognition as incentive (competitive cooperation)
rubrics_metrics.description: The institutional accent on originality makes concern with scientific priority a 'normal' response; competition for priority generates competitive cooperation, after which products are communised and esteem accrues to the producer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize priority and credit as the principal personal/individual reward rather than exclusive proprietary rights. Anti-patterns: priority disputes escalating into personal or nationalistic polemics (e.g., Newton vs. Leibniz).

rubrics_metrics.name: Disinterestedness
rubrics_metrics.description: Disinterestedness is a basic institutional element: not equated with altruism, it denotes an institutional pattern that controls motives so that scientists conform to disinterested norms under threat of sanctions and internalized conscience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether scientists subordinate personal or pecuniary interests to communal standards and whether the institution's structures (peer accountability, incentives) promote disinterested behavior. Anti-patterns: fraud, cultism, self-aggrandisement, exploitation of lay credulity, pseudo-science—particularly where peer control is weak.

rubrics_metrics.name: Peer accountability and rigorous policing / verifiability
rubrics_metrics.description: Scientific activity is subject to exacting scrutiny by fellow experts; the public/testable character of science and peer policing underpin disinterestedness and integrity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess mechanisms of review, replication, and expert scrutiny; where peer control is effective, spurious claims are discouraged. Anti-patterns: erosion of peer control leading to abuse of expert authority or proliferation of pseudo-science.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organized skepticism
rubrics_metrics.description: Organized skepticism is both a methodological and institutional mandate: temporary suspension of judgment and detached scrutiny of beliefs using empirical and logical criteria.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate practices that promote critical scrutiny and reluctance to accept claims without testing. Note conflicts that arise when science challenges ritualized beliefs of other institutions (religion, state, economy); anti-rationalist or centralized political control can limit the scope of organized skepticism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral as well as technical character of scientific norms
rubrics_metrics.description: The mores of science possess a methodologic rationale but are binding also because they are believed to be right and good; they are transmitted by precept and example and reinforced by sanctions, internalized as scientific conscience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assessment should consider both procedural efficiency and the moral legitimation/internalization of norms; note the role of socialization, sanctions, and exemplar behavior in norm maintenance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Openness of careers / meritocratic access
rubrics_metrics.description: The demand that careers be open to talents: restricting scientific careers on grounds other than competence prejudices knowledge and is functionally counterproductive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate recruitment, promotion, and access policies for impartiality and competence-based criteria. Anti-patterns: caste-based exclusion, discrimination masked by ideologies claiming innate incapacity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tension between scientific ethos and wider social/economic institutions
rubrics_metrics.description: Science's institutional imperatives may conflict with non-scientific social structures (political, economic, religious); examples include patents and capitalist property regimes, nationalistic pressures, or totalitarian control.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing scientific practice or policy, identify cases where external institutions impose constraints or incentives that distort scientific norms (e.g., secrecy for commercial advantage, state-directed research suppressing universalism or skepticism). Note documented responses: patenting by scientists, calls for socialism, entrepreneurial promotion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Science-society reciprocity and legitimation during crisis
rubrics_metrics.description: Under attack or in crisis, science must reexamine its foundations, restate objectives, and seek rationale to justify its autonomy and role within society; crisis invites self-appraisal and reaffirmation of the ethos.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate how scientific institutions articulate public justification, adapt governance, and respond to societal challenges (ethical, political) while maintaining core norms. Example: wartime pressures forcing scientists into new social roles.
